issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, bus riding is not impossible but is hard to justify here because the rest of the profile provides no transport-related memory or appraisal content linking the trauma to buses or commuting. With Triggers strongly tied to Negative Appraisals in the formulation, the trigger set should plausibly connect to the appraisal themes; this item appears isolated.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: Self-blame can occur after trauma to a loved one, but in this profile it implies perceived causal responsibility for the loved one's trauma. That responsibility theme is not supported by the memory items, which are mainly sensory re-experiencing, nor by the other trigger content. The appraisal therefore feels insufficiently grounded in the rest of the selected profile.

For trauma to a loved one, 'Entrapment: Having no options' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which centers on victim-focused reminders and guilt about failing to protect others rather than a personal entrapment situation. It implies a different trauma context unless more detail is provided.

issues.item: Memory: Taste Vividness: I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns
issues.explanation: 'Taste Vividness' is difficult to fit with the selected trauma type and the rest of the memory profile. In a loved-one trauma profile with auditory and narrative-fragmentation features, gustatory reliving is possible but here feels disconnected and unusually specific without any other sensory context supporting why taste would be central.

vignette:
Mikaele, a 55-year-old Oceanian man, had built his life around the gentle rhythm of caring for children. For years, he found deep satisfaction as a nanny, a role that allowed him to nurture and protect. Then came the afternoon at the park, an ordinary day that shattered his world. He was supervising little Leilani, a vibrant two-year-old, on a playground slide. In a fraction of a second, she slipped from his sight, falling awkwardly and hitting her head. He remembered the sickening thud, the contorted angle of her tiny arm, and the panicked, guttural cries that were his own, quickly joined by her parents' horrified screams. Leilani didn't survive.

In the aftermath, Mikaele's mind became a battlefield. He wrestled with the memory, but the recollections were fragmented and overwhelming. When he tried to explain what happened, he would lose the thread, the words dissolving into a fog of grief, unable to finish a sentence. Each time he attempted to articulate the sequence of events, his inability to clearly explain what happened only solidified his belief that he was a weak person, someone who had failed catastrophically. This pervasive sense that he should have protected Leilani and that he had failed became a deeply ingrained conviction, haunting his waking hours. He felt like an object, not a person, stripped of his dignity and competence.

This profound conviction that he had failed to protect Leilani and was inherently weak colored every attempt to revisit the event, making it impossible for him to explain what happened clearly. The memories themselves were distorted by the weight of his self-condemnation; sometimes, when he had memories of what happened, he would hear things in his head, the terrifying sounds of that afternoon, amplifying his distress. His pervasive sense of failure to protect and his belief in his own weakness made him acutely sensitive to any potential vulnerability in children, transforming innocuous sights into potent triggers. A child's scraped knee at the park, a brief glimpse of a small hand or foot that reminded him of Leilani's, or even hearing someone talk about people losing loved ones on the radio, could instantly plunge him back into the raw immediacy of his trauma.

These triggers, once activated, would bring an overwhelming wave of grief on recall, a sorrow so profound it felt physical. His fragmented memories, now saturated with this grief, continued to feed his negative appraisals. Each time he tried to piece together the fragmented, grief-laden memories, his inability to articulate the sequence of events coherently only solidified his belief that he was a weak person who had failed in his most fundamental duty. The cycle tightened, his conviction that he was a failure making it harder to process the memories, and the unprocessed, grief-filled memories, in turn, reinforcing his sense of inadequacy.

His divorce, which followed shortly after Leilani's death, was a quiet casualty of his internal struggle. He continued to work as a nanny, drawn by the familiar comfort of children but tormented by the constant echoes of his failure. Every day was a tightrope walk. At his current job, caring for two young siblings, he found himself constantly monitoring them, his eyes drawn to their small body parts as they played, terrified of missing a sign of danger. He would instinctively flinch away from any conversation about loss, his heart pounding in his chest. He lived with the constant internal refrain, "I should have protected others and I failed." Mikaele recently sought help, exhausted by the relentless grip of his past, hoping to finally find a way to live without feeling like an object, constantly defined by a single, tragic moment. He was desperate to understand why he couldn't just "get over it," deeply afraid that his weakness would forever prevent him from truly living again.
